title: Kernel multiplexing contention: INT8 / AWQ mixed-workload scan (field notes)
content:
Purpose:
Quick, messy field notes from a targeted scan to reproduce and quantify the latency tail introduced when multiple quantized kernels are active on the same GPU ("kernel multiplexing"). We focused on AWQ-int8 and a GPTQ-int8 implementation plus an FP8 path to see cross-kernel interference and the cost/quality tradeoffs when requests are arbitrarily mixed by the router.

Summary (short):
- Observation: When routing mixes requests that touch different low-precision kernels, p99 latency increases by 40–140% vs homogeneous runs; throughput drops up to 25% under steady QPS.
- Root suspects: kernel load/unload stalls (driver/context), cache thrash (L2/texture/KV-cache), and scheduler preemption between CUDA kernels compiled with different launch params.
- Quality: AWQ-int8 and GPTQ-int8 have comparable generation-level fidelity for common prompts; divergence occurs on rare-token sequences and arithmetic/structured outputs (AWQ shows a small but measurable increase in token-level disagreement vs fp16).

Hardware / baseline:
- GPUs: 2x A100 80GB (on dedicated nodes), 1x H100 80GB for comparison.
- Baseline model: Llama-2-13b v2 (fp16 baseline).
- Quant variants: AWQ-int8 pack, GPTQ-int8 pack, FP8 simulated kernel (prototype).
- Runtime: internal runtime v0.12.3 with dynamic batching and per-model kernel selection.
- Client load: synthetic replay of production mix: 60% short-chat (seq 64), 30% assistant (seq 512), 10% long context (seq 2048). QPS tuned to target 80% of measured homogeneous throughput.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Homogeneous runs: all requests routed to same kernel variant (AWQ, GPTQ, FP8) — baseline for perf/quality.
- Mixed runs: router randomly mixes kernels per-request (uniform), and routed-by-model (sticky but periodically switched).
- Kernel placement: co-located (same GPU) vs isolated (dedicated GPU per variant).
- Warm/cold: cold start after model unload (measure warm-up penalty), steady-state after 30 min.

Key metrics collected:
- p50/p95/p99 server-side latency (ms) per request type
- tokens/sec throughput (tail-aware)
- kernel switch overhead (measured via in-process tracing; wall-clock between kernel launches for sequential requests touching different kernels)
- generation quality deltas: token disagreement vs fp16 baseline, short-answer BLEU-ish heuristics, sampling-stability score on rare-token prompts

Representative numbers (A100, mixed uniform routing):
- Homogeneous AWQ-int8 steady: p50=34ms, p95=82ms, p99=140ms, throughput=12.6k tok/s
- Homogeneous GPTQ-int8 steady: p50=36ms, p95=88ms, p99=152ms, throughput=12.0k tok/s
- Mixed AWQ+GPTQ uniform: p50=38ms (+5%), p95=115ms (+32%), p99=205ms (+52%), throughput=9.8k tok/s (-22%)
- Mixed AWQ+GPTQ with isolating routing (sticky by session): p50=35ms, p95=90ms, p99=160ms, throughput=11.6k tok/s
- Kernel switch overhead (measured): median 120us, p95 780us, p99 2.6ms — these numbers correlate with spikes when a request triggers a different kernel right before a hot batch.

Quality observations:
- Token disagreement (vs fp16): AWQ-int8 average 1.6% token-level disagreement on short prompts, GPTQ-int8 1.3%; disagreement increases on long-context structural prompts to 3–4% for AWQ vs 2–3% for GPTQ.
- Rare-token prompts (headlines, code tokens): AWQ had 0.7% higher chance of producing mis-ordered punctuation/spacing in generated code snippets; GPTQ produced slightly more conservative token probability mass (less hallucination) in this sample set.
- FP8 prototype showed smallest token disagreement (0.9% short), but its kernel instability and temporary spike cost made it worse in mixed workloads unless isolated.

Hypothesis (mechanics):
1) Kernel binary switching: different kernels use different PTX/launch configs and alter device-side workspace allocations; when the runtime invokes a kernel compiled with different resource usage, the driver inserts implicit synchronization and memory remapping that cost ~0.5–3ms depending on preceding active kernels.
2) Shared L2/texture/KV-cache pressure: AWQ packing strategy tends to access tiled memory patterns that evict other kernels' hot blocks, increasing miss rates on repeated KV accesses across requests.
3) CUDA stream and priority interplay: our runtime currently uses a small set of streams and relies on stream priorities for fairness; mixed kernels with different concurrency patterns cause micro-preemptions that appear as latency jitter.

Repro tips / fast checks: (for on-call or quick replays)
- Reproduce with 1 GPU and low QPS using the mixed-uniform routing flag (--mux-mode=uniform) in the replay harness to force frequent kernel switches.
- Turn on per-kernel tracing: set RUNTIME_TRACE=kernel,launch and capture the 10s window around p99.
- Compare co-located vs isolated by spinning up a second node and using node-affinity in routing.

Mitigations tested (notes):
- Sticky routing (session affinity) dramatically reduces p99 and throughput loss with only small fairness tradeoffs — good quick mitigation.
- Kernel pre-warm: keep all quant kernels resident during heavy windows; reduces cold-swap penalties but does not eliminate inter-kernel eviction costs. Uses extra GPU memory (10–14% overhead).
- Grouped batching by kernel: add a short scheduling window (2–5ms) to batch together same-kernel requests. This gave best p99 reduction but increased p50 slightly for some short-chat traffic.
- Per-kernel CUDA stream pools: reduced micro-preemption; required runtime changes to ensure correct concurrency limits.

Operational recommendations: (short-term vs medium-term)
- Short-term (patchable): enable session affinity for multi-tenant customers with high P99 sensitivity; enable kernel pre-warm during peak windows; add a router parameter to avoid mixing quant-variants on single GPU unless essential.
- Medium-term (engineering): implement profile-guided routing that picks device placement based on quant-kernel affinity and live tail signals; add dynamic grouped batching to the scheduler; add a kernel hotset manager that pins frequently used kernel binaries and pre-allocates workspace.
- Long-term (research): investigate unified kernels that can accept multiple quant formats with a single launch path (reduce binary churn), and explore memory layout harmonization between AWQ and GPTQ packing to reduce eviction interference.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Does H100 behave significantly better for mixed-kernel load? Initial small H100 sample shows lower p99 uplift (25–40% instead of 40–140%) but still present — needs larger run 24h.
- Can we detect "kernel switch storms" in production traces and auto-throttle router mixing before SLA breach? (work queued in JIRA-4567).
- Is there a measurable difference in cost-effectiveness when isolating kernels (wasted GPU capacity) vs accepting higher p99 (customer SLA loss)? We need a cost-SLA simulation.

Appendix (quick command snippets):
- Launch mixed replay: ./replay --profile=prod-mix --mux-mode=uniform --qps=200 --duration=30m
- Capture kernel trace: RUNTIME_TRACE=kernel,launch ./runtime --config=dev.yaml 2>&1 | tee kernel-trace.log

Notes to self: handwritten-ish field notes, leave messy data here then move distilled findings to a short runbook. Ping @evan and @ravi for correlation graphs and extended H100 runs.

-- Marisol
